title: My family
goal: Name family members, show ownership in two ways at once, and say "have" in a language that has no verb "to have".
bekal: form possession with the ending **-n** (*Ainon kirja*) and with possessive endings (*kirjani*)
use *minulla on* to say you have something
name fifteen family members and ask about other people's families

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Perhekuva
dialogs.intro: Aino is looking at a photo on the wall of Budi's room.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Kuka tuo on kuvassa? Onko hän sinun äitisi?
lines.id: Who's that in the picture? Is she your mother?
lines.literal: who that-over-there is in-picture? is-? she your mother-your?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Joo, se on minun äitini. Ja tuo on isäni.
lines.id: Yeah, that's my mother. And that's my father.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: He näyttävät mukavilta. Onko sinulla sisaruksia?

lines.text: Ei oikeastaan. Meillä on iso suku ja paljon serkkuja.

notes: **Possession is stated twice.** *Minun äiti**ni*** — "my mother-my". The front word (*minun*) and the ending (*-ni*) say the same thing. Standard Finnish uses both; the **front** one can be dropped (*äitini* already clearly means "my mother"), the **ending** cannot.

**Except with hän and he.** *Hänen miehe**nsä*** — here the front word is required, because the ending *-nsä* doesn't tell you who the owner is. Without *hänen*, the sentence could mean anyone's husband.

**Onko sinulla — "is there at you".** Finnish has no verb "to have" at all. Instead it uses *olla* (to be) plus the owner in an "at" form: *minulla on* = "at me there is". Russian and Arabic work exactly the same way, and once you're used to it, it feels perfectly logical.

**Sisaruksia and serkkuja take the partitive.** After *onko sinulla* and after *paljon*, the noun is partitive because the number isn't fixed — "siblings (some? one? none?)". Compare *minulla on **yksi** isosisko*, where the number is clear.
**Minulla ei ole** — the negative uses *ei ole*, not *ei on*. The verb *olla* goes back to its stem when negated. This is the first surprise about Finnish negation; the whole story is in Unit 7.

**Naimisissa** literally means "in marriage" — the noun *naimiset* with the ending *-ssa*. The opposite is *naimaton* (unmarried). For "have a boyfriend/girlfriend": *minulla on poikaystävä / tyttöystävä*.

grammars.title: The -n ending: possession
body: One letter that does the whole job of English 's. The owner stands **in front of** the thing, just as in English.
after: ⚠️ *äiti → äidin*: the consonant weakens again. Same pattern: *katu → kadun*, *pöytä → pöydän*, *kauppa → kaupan*.
This *-n* ending also shows up in many other places — in front of words like *kanssa*, and as a marker for a completed object (Unit 11). So learning to form it now pays off many times over.
The word order is **always owner first**: *Ainon kirja*, never *kirja Ainon*. Your English instinct ("Aino's book") is exactly right here — just never use "of" order ("the book of Aino").

grammars.title: Minulla on — how Finnish says "have"
body: Finnish has no verb "to own". Instead, the owner takes the ending **-lla/-llä** ("at"), followed by *on*.

head: Owner
-lla form
Example
Meaning
rows: We have a big extended family.

after: The verb is **always *on***, no matter who the owner is or how many things there are: *minulla on kirja*, *minulla on kirjoja*, *heillä on vauva*. Nothing needs to agree.

To negate: change *on* to **ei ole**, and the thing goes into the partitive — *Minulla **ei ole** auto**a***. Changing the thing's form is required; this is one of the first places where the partitive can't be avoided.
To ask: *Onko sinulla…?* — *Onko sinulla aikaa?* (Do you have time?). Answer by repeating the verb: *On.* / *Ei ole.*

blocks.text: ⚠️ Finnish has two kinds of uncle: **setä** is your **father's** brother, **eno** is your **mother's** brother. There's no such split for aunts — *täti* covers both. English doesn't make this distinction at all, so it's genuinely new; if in doubt, *setä* is safer, since children also use it as a general word for any grown man.

*Mummo* and *vaari* are warm everyday words for grandma and grandpa; *isoäiti* and *isoisä* are more neutral, literally "big mother" and "big father" (much like English "grand-"). There are also *mummi*, *pappa*, and *ukki*, which vary by region and family.

sections.title: The full set of possessive endings

blocks.text: Note that *hän* and *he* use exactly the same ending. That's why the word in front (*hänen* / *heidän*) can't be dropped — it's the only thing that tells them apart.

blocks.title: What you'll actually hear on the street
items: In everyday speech the possessive ending often **disappears completely**, leaving only the front word: *mun äiti* (not *minun äitini*), *sun kirja*, *sen auto*.

Don't copy it yet. This course uses the standard forms because they're understood in every situation, while the casual forms look wrong in formal writing — and Finnish language exams require the standard forms.

blocks.text: Ready-made questions for getting to know someone better: *Onko sinulla perhettä Suomessa?* (Do you have family in Finland?), *Kuinka monta sisarusta sinulla on?* (How many siblings do you have?), *Missä sinun perheesi asuu?* (Where does your family live?).

items: We have a big extended family.
